cards: A decree of Ptolemy V is inscribed in hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek on the Rosetta Stone
The last known hieroglyphic inscription is carved at the temple of Philae
The last known inscription in demotic is written at Philae
Jean-François Champollion announces the decipherment of hieroglyphs
Rome annexes Egypt; its emperors are portrayed on temple walls as pharaohs
The Serapeum of Alexandria is destroyed after the emperor Theodosius bans pagan sacrifice
The last known hieroglyphic inscription is carved at the temple of Philae
The Third Dynasty begins; its first king Djoser orders the Step Pyramid at Saqqara, the work of his vizier Imhotep.
Sneferu founds the Fourth Dynasty, holds territory from Libya to Sinai and Nubia, and builds the Meidum, Bent and Red Pyramids.
Khufu commissions the Great Pyramid of Giza, in which the fully developed pyramid style is reached.
Userkaf founds the Fifth Dynasty, marked by the growing cult of Ra and the sun temples of Abusir.
Unas, the last king of the Fifth Dynasty, has the Pyramid Texts inscribed in his pyramid, the earliest ruler to do so.
Pepi II begins his long reign (2278–2214 BCE), during which internal disorder sets in.
The Sixth Dynasty ends; drought, famine and civil war open the First Intermediate Period.
Amid earthquakes in northern Egypt, casing stones stripped from the pyramid are said to have been carted away for use in nearby Cairo
Cyriacus of Ancona visits Giza and refutes the medieval belief that the pyramids were the granaries of Joseph
Howard Vyse opens the four upper relieving chambers, whose painted work-gang names spell out Khufu’s names
Kamal el-Mallakh finds a sealed boat pit at the south foot of the pyramid holding the dismantled Khufu ship
The ScanPyramids project detects a large cavity above the Grand Gallery, the “Big Void”, whose purpose is unknown
Charles Bonnet’s Swiss team finds a cache of granite statues of the Twenty-fifth Dynasty pharaohs at Kerma
Thutmose III defeats a Canaanite coalition at Megiddo after a daring march through the Aruna pass
Ramesses II fights the Hittite king Muwatalli II to a draw at the Battle of Kadesh
Egypt and the Hittites conclude a peace treaty acknowledging strategic stalemate
He succeeds his father Seti I as pharaoh at the age of 25
He fights the Hittite forces of Muwatalli II at Kadesh in Syria, a battle generally considered a stalemate
Returning to Syria, his armies take Moab and recapture Upi, the land around Damascus
He concludes the peace known as the Treaty of Kadesh with the Hittite king Ḫattušili III
With his queen Nefertari he travels into Nubia to inaugurate the temple of Abu Simbel
He dies aged about 90, early in his 67th regnal year, and is succeeded by his son Merneptah
The Assyrian king Esarhaddon takes Memphis
Ashurbanipal's army sacks Thebes, ending Kushite rule in Egypt
The Garamantes join Oea against Leptis Magna and are driven back by Valerius Festus
The Vandal conquest of North Africa begins, disrupting Mediterranean trade demand
Elissa (Dido) of Tyre traditionally founds Carthage
The Barcid family begins the conquest of southern Iberia
Hannibal crosses the Alps and invades Italy
Hannibal annihilates a Roman army at Cannae
Scipio Aemilianus storms and razes Carthage, ending the Third Punic War
Ptolemy becomes satrap of Egypt after the death of Alexander the Great
Ptolemy I Soter proclaims himself king, founding the dynasty
Ptolemy II Philadelphus begins his reign over an empire reaching Cyprus and the Aegean
Ptolemy IV defeats Antiochus III at Raphia with a phalanx of native Egyptians
Priests issue the decree later inscribed on the Rosetta Stone
Octavian defeats Cleopatra VII and Mark Antony at Actium
Rome annexes Egypt, ending the Ptolemaic state
After the assassination of Hasdrubal, Hannibal is proclaimed commander-in-chief by the army in Iberia at the age of 26
He leaves New Carthage in late spring, crosses the Pyrenees, the Rhône and the Alps, and enters Italy
He destroys the army of the consul Gaius Flaminius in an ambush on the shore of Lake Trasimene
At Cannae he surrounds a Roman army, of which 50,000–70,000 are estimated killed or captured
He marches on Rome to draw off the besiegers of Capua, but the city falls to the Romans
After nearly 15 years in Italy he is recalled to Carthage to defend it against Scipio Africanus
Scipio defeats him at the Battle of Zama, the last major battle of the Second Punic War
Commanding a Seleucid fleet for Antiochus III, he is forced to retreat by the Rhodian navy at the Battle of Side
Masinissa leaves Carthage and allies with Scipio
Masinissa's cavalry helps Rome win the Battle of Zama; Numidia is united
Masinissa defeats Carthage, giving Rome a pretext for the Third Punic War
Masinissa dies; royal powers are divided among his sons
Jugurtha takes Cirta and kills Adherbal and Italian traders
Bocchus I hands Jugurtha over to Sulla
Caesar defeats Juba I at Thapsus and creates the province of Africa Nova
Rome destroys Carthage and creates the province of Africa, governed from Utica
Caesar annexes Numidian lands as Africa Nova after Thapsus
A revolt at Thysdrus proclaims Gordian I emperor
The Vandals under Gaiseric seize Carthage
Cleopatra is born to Ptolemy XII Auletes, probably in the early part of the year
Her father dies and she begins her reign, at first alongside her brother Ptolemy XIII
Driven from Alexandria by her brother's party, she returns with an army and meets Julius Caesar in the palace
Ptolemy XIII drowns in the Nile, Caesar makes her joint ruler with Ptolemy XIV, and she gives birth to Caesarion
She sails to Tarsos to meet Mark Antony, who follows her to Alexandria
At the Donations of Alexandria she and her children are declared rulers of lands under Antony's authority
Octavian's fleet under Agrippa defeats hers and Antony's at the Battle of Actium
Octavian takes Alexandria; Antony and then Cleopatra commit suicide
Octavian takes Alexandria; Antony and Cleopatra VII die
The Constitutio Antoniniana makes most free Egyptians Roman citizens
Council of Chalcedon; most Egyptian Christians reject its creed
Alexandria is surrendered by treaty to the Rashidun Caliphate
Gaiseric leads the Vandals and Alans across from Hispania to Africa and besieges Hippo Regius, where Saint Augustine dies on 28 August 430.
A treaty with Valentinian III grants the Vandals coastal Numidia and parts of Mauretania.
Gaiseric breaks the treaty, captures Carthage without a fight and makes it his capital.
A second treaty gives the Vandals Byzacena, Tripolitania and part of Numidia and confirms their hold on Proconsular Africa.
The Vandals sack Rome, carrying off the empress Licinia Eudoxia, her daughters and the spoils of the Temple in Jerusalem.
At Cape Bon the Vandals destroy the Western fleet and part of the Eastern fleet sent to overthrow them.
Gaiseric dies at 88; his son Huneric succeeds and from 482 persecutes Nicene Christians and Manichaeans.
Gelimer, besieged at Mount Pappua after the defeats at Ad Decimum and Tricamarum, surrenders to the Byzantines.
Makurian archers repel an Arab raid sent from newly conquered Egypt
Siege of Old Dongola ends with the Baqt treaty with Muslim Egypt
Turan-Shah, brother of Saladin, sacks Qasr Ibrim
A Mamluk army defeats King David and installs a tributary king
The Throne Hall at Old Dongola is converted into a mosque
John of Ephesus mentions Alodia for the first time, as a kingdom on the cusp of Christianization.
Longinus is sent at the king's request and baptizes him, his family and the nobility; Alodia joins the Coptic Patriarchate of Alexandria.
Makuria and the Arabs sign the Baqt after two failed invasions; the treaty explicitly leaves Alodia unaffected.
The Damadim attack Nubia from the south, according to Ibn Sa'id al-Maghribi; Soba may have been conquered and destroyed.
Al-Abwab, the northernmost province, is recorded as an independent splinter kingdom.
Soba lies in ruins; Abdallah Jammah and the Funj king Amara Dunqas destroy the kingdom, and the Funj found Sennar.
Idris ibn Abdallah, fleeing the Abbasids after the Battle of Fakhkh, settles at Volubilis, where the Awraba Berbers make him their imam.
Idris I is poisoned by an Abbasid agent; his posthumous son Idris II is brought up under the regency of the freedman Rashid.
Idris II has the Awraba leader Ishak killed and moves his seat from Walili to Fez, founding the settlement of al-'Aliya.
Idris II dies; the state reaches from western Algeria to the Sous, and his son Muhammad divides it among seven brothers.
The Sufri Kharijite tribes of Madyuna, Ghayata and Miknasa defeat Ali ibn Umar and occupy Fez until Yahya III retakes it.
Musa ibn Abul 'Afiya of the Miknasa captures and kills Hassan I al-Hajam: the Idrisids never again hold Fez.
The Umayyad general Ghalib expels the Idrisids from their lands and takes al-Hasan and other Idrisids as hostages to Córdoba.
Harun al-Rashid appoints Ibrahim I ibn al-Aghlab hereditary emir of Ifriqiya; he founds al-Abbasiyya outside Kairouan.
The Arab jund revolts under Mansur ibn Nasr al-Tunbudhi and occupies Tunis and Kairouan; Ziyadat Allah I crushes the rebellion in 827 with Ibadi Berber help.
Asad ibn al-Furat leads the Aghlabid conquest of Sicily, invited by the Byzantine rebel Euphemios.
Ziyadat Allah I completely rebuilds the Great Mosque of Kairouan.
Ibrahim II moves his residence from al-Abbasiyya to the new palace-city of Raqqada.
Ibrahim II dies besieging Cosenza; Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i takes Mila, the first blow to Aghlabid rule in Africa.
The Kutama rout the Aghlabid army near al-Aribus on 18 March; Ziyadat Allah III flees to Egypt and Abu Abdallah enters Raqqada on 25 March.
Abdallah al-Mahdi Billah is proclaimed caliph at Raqqada after the Kutama overthrow the Aghlabids
General Jawhar al-Siqilli conquers Egypt; Cairo is founded north of Fustat
The al-Azhar mosque is begun, later developing into a great teaching institution
Badr al-Jamali arrives and takes over as vizier and commander after years of chaos
Succession crisis over Nizar splits the Ismaili community permanently
Saladin restores prayers for the Abbasid caliph; the last Fatimid caliph al-Adid dies
Yusuf ibn Tashfin shatters Alfonso VI's army at the Battle of Sagrajas
Almoravids absorb the taifa kingdom of Seville
Death of Yusuf ibn Tashfin, the empire's greatest ruler
Alfonso I of Aragon takes Zaragoza
Tashfin ibn Ali dies near Oran, opening Morocco to the Almohads
Almohads storm Marrakesh and kill the last Almoravid ruler, Ishaq ibn Ali
Ibn Tumart is proclaimed the Mahdi by his followers in the Atlas Mountains
Abd al-Mu'min captures the Almoravid capital Marrakesh and takes the title of caliph
Almohads complete the conquest of the Maghreb from Morocco to Tunisia
Abu Yaqub Yusuf I absorbs the last independent Muslim principality of al-Andalus
Yaqub al-Mansur crushes Alfonso VIII of Castile at the Battle of Alarcos
Christian coalition shatters the Almohad army at Las Navas de Tolosa
Ferdinand III of Castile takes Seville
The last caliph, Idris al-Wathiq, is killed as the Marinids seize Marrakesh
Abu Zakariya Yahya breaks with the Almohad caliph and rules Ifriqiya independently from Tunis
Al-Mustansir takes the caliphal title of commander of the faithful
Louis IX of France dies near Tunis during the Eighth Crusade
Ibn Khaldun is born in Tunis
The Marinid sultan Abu al-Hasan briefly occupies Tunis
Charles V takes Tunis and makes the Hafsid sultan a Spanish vassal
Sinan Pasha’s Ottoman forces take Tunis and end the dynasty
Abu Yahya's reign begins; between 1244 and 1248 the Marinids take Taza, Rabat, Salé, Meknes and Fez from the weakened Almohads.
Abu Yusuf Yaqub captures Marrakesh, effectively ending Almohad rule.
Fes Jdid, 'New Fez', is founded as the dynasty's administrative and military centre.
The Marinids hold Rota, Tarifa and Gibraltar, seeking control of the Strait's trade from Algeciras.
Abu al-Hasan conquers the Abdalwadid kingdom of Tlemcen.
A Portuguese–Castilian army defeats the Marinids at the Battle of Río Salado near Tarifa.
Abu al-Hasan defeats the Hafsids of Ifriqiya and rules from southern Morocco to Tripoli; within a year a revolt of Arab tribes in southern Tunisia costs him the east.
Abd al-Haqq II, the last Marinid sultan, is killed in a revolt in Fez after appointing a Jewish vizier, Aaron ben Batash.
Ibn Khaldun is born in Tunis into the Banū Khaldūn, a family that had left Seville a century earlier
After Tunis is defeated by the sultan of Constantine he follows his teacher al-Ābilī to Fez
His scheming against the Marinid sultan Abū Inan earns him a prison sentence of 22 months
Muhammad V of Granada sends him to Pedro the Cruel of Castile to endorse a peace treaty
He returns to Tunis after more than three years at Qalat Ibn Salama, where he wrote the Muqaddimah
The Egyptian sultan Barquq makes him a professor and Grand qadi of the Maliki school in Cairo
He negotiates with Timur outside besieged Damascus
He dies a month after his sixth appointment as Maliki qadi
Amara Dunqas founds Sennar, according to tradition
Funj forces defeat the Ethiopian emperor Iyasu II on the Dinder River
Hamaj regents take power after deposing Badi IV
Badi VII submits to the Egyptian army of Ismail Kamil Pasha
The tribes of the Sus proclaim Muhammad al-Qa’im leader of the holy war against Portugal
Muhammad al-Shaykh takes Agadir from the Portuguese
The Saadis take Fez from the Wattasids
Victory over Sebastian of Portugal at the Battle of Alcácer Quibir
Judar Pasha defeats Songhai at the Battle of Tondibi
Death of Ahmad al-Mansur and start of civil war among his sons
Morisco corsairs found the Republic of Salé
The last Saadi sultan is killed in Marrakesh
The corsair Oruç Barbarossa seizes Algiers
Hayreddin captures the Spanish fort on the Peñón and builds the harbour mole
Charles V’s expedition against Algiers is wrecked by a storm and repulsed
The corsair captains impose the first dey
Algiers takes Oran from Spain, losing it in 1732 and recovering it in 1792
An Anglo-Dutch fleet under Lord Exmouth bombards Algiers
French troops land at Sidi Ferruch and Algiers capitulates on 5 July
French troops land at Sidi Ferruch and Algiers capitulates on 5 July
Abdelkader surrenders to French forces after fifteen years of resistance
Northern Algeria is divided into the French departments of Algiers, Oran and Constantine
The Crémieux Decree grants French citizenship to Algerian Jews
The Mokrani revolt is crushed and followed by large land confiscations
The Sétif and Guelma massacres follow riots on 8 May
The FLN launches the war of independence on 1 November
The Évian Accords end the war and Algeria becomes independent on 5 July
On 18 June the monarchy is abolished and Egypt declared a republic, with Muhammad Naguib as president and Gamal Abdel Nasser as prime minister.
Nasser becomes president in June, the last British troops leave the Canal Zone on 13 June, and on 26 July he nationalises the Suez Canal, provoking the Suez Crisis.
In the Six-Day War Israel captures the Sinai Peninsula and the Gaza Strip; an Emergency Law expanding police powers is enacted and stays in force until 2012.
Sadat coordinates with Syria in the Fourth Arab-Israeli War to reclaim Sinai, restoring Arab morale and his own legitimacy.
The Egypt–Israel peace treaty is signed after Sadat's 1977 visit to Jerusalem; Egypt is temporarily expelled from the Arab League.
Sadat is assassinated by an Islamic extremist; Hosni Mubarak succeeds him in a referendum in which he is the sole candidate.
After 18 days of protests centred on Tahrir Square, Mubarak resigns on 11 February and the military takes control.
The military removes President Mohamed Morsi on 3 July; the dispersal of pro-Morsi camps on 14 August kills 595, the deadliest day in modern Egyptian history.
Sultan Mohammed V, restored from exile in 1955 and sovereign of an independent Morocco since March 1956, takes the title of King.
Hassan II becomes King on 3 March; he holds the first general elections in 1963, then declares a state of emergency and suspends parliament in 1965.
On 6 November some 350,000 civilians cross into the Spanish Sahara in the Green March; Spain cedes the territory to Morocco and Mauritania and Moroccan forces occupy it.
A UN-monitored ceasefire ends fifteen years of war with the Polisario Front in Western Sahara, leaving the territory's status undecided.
Hassan II dies and is succeeded by his son Mohammed VI, who sets up the Equity and Reconciliation Commission to examine his father's abuses.

Thousands rally for reform during the Arab Spring; the King wins a landslide in a July referendum on a new constitution, and the Justice and Development Party's Abdelilah Benkirane heads the government.
On 10 December Morocco normalises relations with Israel, and the United States becomes the first Western state to back Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara.
After the general election of 23 September, Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri is appointed the first woman prime minister on 29 September.
